items.title: Assert Test
items.text:
Assert Test was created to test scenes using Godot built-in assert.

Warning

It's not a replacement for full-featured unit testing addons like GdUnit or Gut!

items.title: For who is it?
items.text:
It's for people that don't want to spend a lot of time learning a test framework.

In my case I spent time reading two test frameworks to decide which is my style 🫠

It works by running a scene in a new process and collecting it's stderr to know if something gone wrong. Of course, there is downsides for doing things that way and you can read at downsides.

items.title: Downsides
items.text: I use this page to register negative sides of this addon (because it's not a bed of roses).

items.title: Test cost
items.text:
To test a scene we need to create many things (a process, a thread, a mutex, a timer) and these increase the cost of making one single test.

My recommendation is: Go crazy with the asserts and test as much as possible in a single scene.

items.title: Detailed information
items.text:
We use stderr to identify if an error occurred and that's it. We can't tell you details like:

  • How many assert errors
  • How many memory leak errors
  • How many an assert failed
  • ...

If you want to know the error, you need to read the stderr.

Other test frameworks

They are able to get details because they introduce their own asserts, so they are the ones collecting the error and registering informations.

GutGdUnit4TinyTest

~54 assert methods.

  • assert_eq(variable, 10)
  • assert_true(variable)
  • assert_null(variable)
  • ...

~14 assert methods (which expand in more validations).

  • assert_int(variable).is_equal(10)
  • assert_bool(variable).is_true()
  • assert_array(variable).is_empty()
  • ...

1 assert method.

  • TinyTest.assert_true(true, "message")

items.title: False fail
items.text:
If the presence of stderr is what indicates failing, then anyone can trigger a fail with:

  • printerr()
  • push_warning()
  • push_error()
  • manually writing to stderr

Imagine that a plugin that you use has an tolerable error, it would generate an stderr and, consequently, mark your test as failed.

items.title: Feature limitation
items.text:
If you are senior tester, you probably will not like the fact that we don't have many features like:

  • Test discovery
  • Test setup and teardown
  • Test doubles
  • Assertion library
  • ...

If you can imagine, we probably don't have it.

items.title: Memory Leak
items.text:
Is a classic problem that people normally don't notice until closing the game, because it's only then that Godot shows in the terminal a message like: 

WARNING: 1 ObjectDB instance was leaked at exit (run with `--verbose` for details).
    at: cleanup (core/object/object.cpp:2536)

Godot has three objects that interact with memory in a different way:

  • Object
  • Node
  • RefCounted

items.title: Object
items.text:
The classic "you allocated, you free it".

Memory leakFix 
func _ready() -> void:
    var a := Object.new()

    get_tree().quit()

func _ready() -> void:
    var a := Object.new()

    a.free()

    get_tree().quit()

items.title: Cautions
items.text:
If your object is built from others objects, you need to remember to free every single one.

Memory leakFix 
func _ready() -> void:
    var a := Example.new()

    get_tree().quit()


class Example extends Object:
    var b := Object.new()

func _ready() -> void:
    var a := Example.new()

    a.b.free()
    a.free()

    get_tree().quit()


class Example extends Object:
    var b := Object.new()

items.title: Node
items.text:
When you free it, it will free the descedants before itself.

Memory leakFix 
func _ready() -> void:
    var a := Node.new()
    var b := Node.new()

    a.add_child(b)

    get_tree().quit()

func _ready() -> void:
    var a := Node.new()
    var b := Node.new()

    a.add_child(b)
    a.free()

    get_tree().quit()

items.title: Cautions
items.text:
If you remove a Node from it parent, you have to remember to manually free it later.

Memory leakFix 
func _ready() -> void:
    var a := Node.new()
    var b := Node.new()

    a.add_child(b)
    a.remove_child(b)

    get_tree().quit()

func _ready() -> void:
    var a := Node.new()
    var b := Node.new()

    a.add_child(b)
    a.remove_child(b)
    a.free()
    b.free()

    get_tree().quit()

Do not confuse children with properties, a Node in the property needs to freed manually.

Memory leakFix 
func _ready() -> void:
    var a := Example.new()

    a.free()

    get_tree().quit()


class Example extends Node:
    var b := Node.new()

func _ready() -> void:
    var a := Example.new()

    a.b.free()
    a.free()

    get_tree().quit()


class Example extends Node:
    var b := Node.new()

items.title: RefCounted
items.text:
It will free itself when no one reference it anymore. 

func _ready() -> void:
    var a := RefCounted.new()

    get_tree().quit()

items.title: Cautions
items.text:
Avoid circular reference, otherwise it will never free itself.

Memory leakFix 
func _ready() -> void:
    var a := Example.new()
    var b := Example.new()

    a.r = b
    b.r = a

    get_tree().quit()


class Example extends RefCounted:
    var r: RefCounted = null

func _ready() -> void:
    var a := Example.new()
    var b := Example.new()

    a.r = weakref(b)
    b.r = weakref(a)

    get_tree().quit()


class Example extends RefCounted:
    var r: WeakRef = null

WeakRef will not increase the reference count and to get back the reference use get_ref().

Losing the autocomplete

WeakRef.get_ref() returns a Variant, which means that you lose the autocomplete and needs to convert back to the correct type. One way that to solve this (instead of always converting) is to create an intermediary class like: 

func _ready() -> void:
    var a := Example.new()
    var b := Example.new()

    a.r = RefExample.new(b)
    b.r = RefExample.new(a)

    get_tree().quit()


class Example extends RefCounted:
    var r: RefExample = null


class RefExample extends RefCounted:
    var r: WeakRef = null

    func _init(e: Example) -> void:
        r = weakref(e)

    func get_ref() -> Example:
        return r.get_ref() as Example

items.title: Quitting
items.text:
A very important part of these tests is knowing how to quit(). So pay attention to these details:

  • quit(): Will quit the application at the end of current iteration
  • assert(): Failing will make the function return but the application continues running

items.title: Avoid assert() before quit()
items.text:
The following code will never call the quit() because the assert() will fail and make the function return. 

func _ready() -> void:
    assert(false)

    # Never called.
    get_tree().quit()

But the next code will work because quit() continues with the function code: 

func _ready() -> void:
    get_tree().quit()

    # Called.
    assert(false)

An alternative is letting the assert() code inside functions, so it continues after breaking. 

func _ready() -> void:
    example()

    # Called.
    get_tree().quit()


func example() -> void:
    assert(false)

Info

This is not unique of assert(), Godot handle unexpected erros by making the function return the default value.

items.title: Always adjust timeout
items.text:
An error can happen in any part of your code and happening before a quit() is the worst possible case, because you will never send the request to close the test. For example: 

func _ready() -> void:
    var x = 10
    var y = Object.new()

    print(x + y)

    # Never called.
    get_tree().quit()

To avoid letting the process running forever, AssertScene includes a property timeout to halt the process after some seconds (default is 3 seconds). You will know that your test was halted because we add a message to your report: 

(FAIL) Test description here --- Scene halted after exceeding time limit
    SCRIPT ERROR: Invalid operands 'int' and 'Object' in operator '+'.
              at: _ready (res://tests/scenes/test_name.gd:8)
              GDScript backtrace (most recent call first):
                  [0] _ready (res://tests/scenes/test_name.gd:8)

Note

Notice how you still receive any stderr that we collect during this time, so you can still indentify the problem.

The important part is to remember to adjust to an adequate value for longer tests.

items.title: Creating a test
items.text:
• Create a scene to be tested
  • Add as many assert() you wanto to validate if everything is working right
  • End the scene with get_tree().quit()

Note

Notice how we didn't use any feature from the addon to create the test.

  • Our scene doesn't have a Node from the addon
  • Our files doesn't need prefix/suffix test
  • Our methods doesn't need prefix/suffix test
  • Our script doesn't have to extend an addon script
  • Our script doesn't call method from the addon

The test is just a scene that close itself!

items.title: Running a test
items.text:
The first step is to create a scene which will be responsible for running your test scenes. It should have an AssertReport with one or more AssertScene as children.

Info

  • AssertReport initiate the children tests and print their results
  • AssertScene run the test scene in a new process

Access your AssertScene properties and put your test scene in the scene property.

Save this scene and execute it to start the tests! Your output should be something like:

No errorAssert failTimeoutedMemory leak 
(OK) Test description here
(1 OK, 0 FAIL)

(FAIL) Test description here
    SCRIPT ERROR: Assertion failed: assert message here
            ...

(0 OK, 1 FAIL)

(FAIL) Test description here --- Scene halted after exceeding time limit

(0 OK, 1 FAIL)

(FAIL) Test description here
    WARNING: 1 ObjectDB instance was leaked at exit (run with `--verbose` for details).
        at: cleanup (core/object/object.cpp:2536)

(0 OK, 1 FAIL)

It's basically the result of your test scene and the stderr messages.

items.title: Running multiple tests
items.text:
To run multiple tests, just add more AssertScene to your scene.

If you have many tests and wants to organize them, you can put AssertReport inside AssertReport.
